analysis.one_liner: Bars banks from forcing fraud claims on credit card and bank accounts into arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced a bill that would make arbitration clauses in credit card and bank account contracts unenforceable for fraud disputes that had not yet been decided by a court — the kind of clauses banks like Wells Fargo used after the fake-accounts scandal to push customers out of court (S2, S3). The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action for the rest of the Congress (S5).
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with credit cards or personal bank accounts who discover fraud — for example, unauthorized accounts or charges. The bill's findings say courts have held that even customers suing over fake accounts opened without their consent were still bound to arbitration under their account contracts, leaving them "no meaningful choice" (S3). The bill would let those claims be heard in court instead (S2, S3).

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Truth in Lending Act and the Bank Holding Company Act so that an arbitration agreement cannot block a dispute related to a credit card account or personal bank account that is not subject to a final court judgment (S2, S3).

Its stated purpose is to ensure financial institutions cannot use arbitration clauses to escape accountability for fraud; the bill's findings cite the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Wells Fargo enforcement action covering millions of unauthorized accounts and credit card enrollments (S3).
It applies only to credit card and bank accounts not issued in response to a consumer's request, targeting accounts opened without the customer's knowledge (S2).

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit card issuers, which would face more fraud claims litigated in open court, with higher legal costs and potentially larger judgments, and the arbitration industry, which loses that stream of cases.

drawbacks.text: Opponents of arbitration limits generally argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than court litigation and that wider class actions raise costs for all customers, not just claimants; the bill text records the industry-favored framing that customers agreed to arbitration in their account contracts (S3).

The bill is narrow: it only covers credit card and personal bank account disputes not already decided by a court, so fraud on other products — mortgages, auto loans, brokerage accounts — would still be forced into arbitration (S2, S3).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers who discover fraud, the benefit is substantial — access to court instead of a private forum where the bank chooses the arbitrator, and where courts have held even fake-account victims must arbitrate (S3). The cost falls on banks in the form of litigation exposure and on customers in the form of potentially higher fees spread across accounts. The bill never advanced far enough for a committee report, so its precise scope and any limits were never refined.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 7, 2017 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services (S1, S5).
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019 (S5).
The bill had 25 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no bipartisan co-sponsorship (S4).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit card issuers that rely on arbitration clauses to channel fraud claims away from court, and the arbitration industry, are better off because the bill never advanced; consumers who sign account agreements keep the same clauses in their contracts.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.role: Lead sponsor; drafted the bill responding to the Wells Fargo fake-accounts scandal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction controlled by the majority
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or marked up the bill; it died there

against.name: Financial services and arbitration industries
against.role: Industries whose account-contract arbitration clauses the bill would invalidate
against.what_they_did: No position appears in the congressional record, but they are the interests the bill directly burdens; banking groups generally opposed limits on arbitration during this period

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 25 cosponsors were all Democrats (S4), and the majority-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action on it (S5), so the outcome tracks party lines — but no roll-call votes were ever held on the bill itself.

industries.note: The bill would invalidate the arbitration clauses these institutions write into credit card and bank account contracts, exposing them to fraud claims in court instead of private arbitration. Its findings directly cite the Wells Fargo fake-accounts case, where such clauses kept fraud claims out of court (S3).
Arbitration firms and the law practices built around bank-mandated arbitration would lose the stream of credit card and bank account fraud disputes the bill would send to court instead.
